note: Plain definitions. aka = other spellings the Reading Room looks for when it underlines terms in an abstract.

terms.d: A flat, spinning disc of gas spiralling into a massive object. Friction heats the gas, so the disc can outshine everything around it. Discs feed black holes, neutron stars and newborn stars.
The centre of a galaxy whose supermassive black hole is being fed. The infalling gas shines across the whole spectrum and can outshine all the galaxy's stars. Quasars are the brightest kind.
A unit of angle on the sky: 1/3,600 of a degree. A small coin seen from 4 km away covers about one arcsecond. A milliarcsecond is a thousandth of that and a microarcsecond a millionth.
The average distance from Earth to the Sun: 149,597,870.7 km. Light crosses it in 8 minutes 19 seconds.
Something measurable, such as a gas in an atmosphere or a molecule in a sample, that living things produce and that is hard to make any other way. None has yet been confirmed beyond Earth.

A region where gravity is strong enough that nothing, including light, can get out. Stellar ones form when massive stars collapse; supermassive ones, millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, sit at the centres of galaxies.
A giant star that swells and shrinks on a regular cycle of days to months. The longer the cycle, the more luminous the star, so timing one gives its true brightness and therefore its distance.

How far away a distant galaxy is right now, allowing for the space that has stretched while its light was travelling. It is larger than the light-travel distance: the most distant light we see has travelled 13.8 billion years, from matter that is now about 46 billion light-years away.
A mask inside a telescope that blocks a star's light so that faint things next to it, such as planets or dust discs, can be seen.

The distance beyond which light emitted today will never reach us, because the space in between is expanding too fast. It lies about 16 to 17 billion light-years away. We can still see older light from galaxies now beyond it.
Light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe first became transparent. It has since been stretched into microwaves at 2.7255 K and arrives from every direction.
The name for whatever is making the expansion of the universe speed up. It behaves like energy built into empty space and makes up about 68% of the universe's contents. Its nature is unknown.
Matter that has gravity but neither emits nor absorbs light. It outweighs ordinary matter about five to one and holds galaxies and clusters together. No particle of it has been detected directly.

How much a radio pulse has been smeared by the free electrons it passed through: low frequencies arrive later than high. A large value means a long path, which is how fast radio bursts were shown to come from other galaxies.
The surface around a black hole from inside which nothing can return. It is a boundary in space, with nothing solid there.
A flash of radio waves lasting about a thousandth of a second, from another galaxy. Some repeat, most are seen once. At least some come from magnetars.

Light from an atomic transition so unlikely that, at laboratory densities, collisions always interrupt it first. In the near-vacuum of a nebula it has time to happen. The teal glow of doubly ionised oxygen at 500.7 nm, written [O III], is the best known.
A flash of gamma rays lasting from milliseconds to minutes, for that time the brightest thing in the universe. Long ones come from collapsing massive stars, short ones from merging neutron stars.
A tight ball of hundreds of thousands of old stars orbiting a galaxy. The Milky Way has about 160. Most are over 10 billion years old.
Mass bends the path of light. A galaxy or cluster between us and a more distant object can magnify, distort or multiply its image, which also lets astronomers weigh the lens, dark matter included.
A ripple in the shape of space, made when massive objects accelerate, travelling at the speed of light. Those detected so far come from pairs of black holes or neutron stars spiralling together.
Gases that let sunlight in but absorb the heat a planet radiates back, warming its surface. On Earth it adds about 33 °C. On Venus it adds more than 500.
Deep red light at 656.28 nm, emitted when the electron in a hydrogen atom drops from its third energy level to its second. It is the colour of glowing nebulae, and the accent colour of this site.
The range of distances from a star where a rocky planet with an atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface. It says nothing about whether a given planet actually has water, air or life.
The edge of the Sun's bubble, where the solar wind is stopped by the thin gas between the stars. Voyager 1 crossed it at 121 AU in 2012 and Voyager 2 at 119 AU in 2018.

The present expansion rate of the universe: how much faster a galaxy recedes for each extra megaparsec of distance. Measured from the early universe it is about 67 km/s per megaparsec, and from nearby supernovae about 73. The mismatch is unexplained.
A body passing through the Solar System that is not bound to the Sun and came from another star system. Three are known: 1I/ʻOumuamua (2017), 2I/Borisov (2019) and 3I/ATLAS (2025).
A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, from about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun. Pluto is its best-known member. It is the source of many short-period comets.
One of five places near two orbiting bodies where a small object keeps station with them. Sun–Earth L2, 1.5 million km beyond Earth, is where the Webb telescope sits.

The standard model of cosmology: a universe that began hot and dense and now consists of about 5% ordinary matter, 27% cold dark matter (CDM) and 68% dark energy (Lambda). It fits nearly every large-scale observation with six numbers.
The distance light travels in a year: 9.46 trillion km, or 63,241 AU. It is a distance, though on this site it doubles as a time: something 100 light-years away is seen as it was 100 years ago.

How long ago the light we now see left its source. For nearby things it equals the distance in light-years. For very distant galaxies it is less than the present distance, because space has stretched since.

A neutron star with a magnetic field a thousand times stronger than an ordinary pulsar's, about a hundred million million times Earth's. When the field shifts, the star's crust cracks and releases bursts of X-rays and radio waves.

The astronomer's brightness scale, which runs backwards: smaller numbers are brighter. Five magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness. The faintest stars visible to the eye are about magnitude 6. Absolute magnitude is how bright something would look from 32.6 light-years.
The long, stable middle of a star's life, when it shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. The Sun is about halfway through 10 billion years of it.
A nearly massless particle with no electric charge that passes through ordinary matter almost untouched. About 65 billion from the Sun's core cross every square centimetre of you each second.
The collapsed core left when a massive star explodes: more than the Sun's mass packed into a ball about 20 km across. A teaspoonful would weigh several hundred million tonnes.

How long a signal travelling at the speed of light takes to cover a distance in one direction. Mission controllers use it every day: it is why a Mars rover cannot be steered live. It is the idea this site is organised around.
A vast, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies thought to surround the Sun from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU, the source of long-period comets. Nothing has been observed while in it.

The apparent shift of a nearby star against the background as Earth moves from one side of its orbit to the other. The shift gives the distance directly, by trigonometry, with no assumptions about the star.
3.26 light-years: the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond. Astronomers use kiloparsecs (thousands) inside galaxies and megaparsecs (millions) between them.
The edge of the observable universe: the present distance to the farthest matter whose light has had time to reach us since the Big Bang. About 46 billion light-years in every direction.
A galaxy's own motion through space, left over once the overall expansion of the universe is subtracted. It comes from the pull of nearby concentrations of mass.
Before a journal publishes a paper, other specialists check it and can ask for changes. 'Submitted to' means that has not happened yet; 'accepted' or 'published in' means it has.
A glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying Sun-like star and lit by the hot core left behind. It has nothing to do with planets; the name comes from how they looked in early telescopes.
The first generation of stars, made only of the hydrogen and helium left by the Big Bang. They are predicted to have been massive and short-lived. None has yet been seen directly.
A paper posted publicly before, or instead of, formal publication in a journal. Nearly all astronomy papers appear first on arXiv.org, free to read. A preprint may still change after review.
A disc of gas and dust around a newborn star, in which planets form over a few million years. A debris disc is the dusty remains left after the gas has gone.

A spinning neutron star whose radio beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse, giving a pulse each turn. Periods run from 1.4 milliseconds to several seconds, and the best keep time as well as atomic clocks.

A set of very stable pulsars across the sky, timed for years. A passing gravitational wave makes some pulses arrive early and others late in a recognisable pattern, turning the Galaxy into a detector.

The brilliant core of a distant galaxy, powered by gas falling into a supermassive black hole. A quasar can outshine its whole galaxy a thousand times over from a region not much bigger than the Solar System.
Motion directly toward or away from us, measured from the Doppler shift of lines in a spectrum. A star that wobbles regularly in radial velocity has something orbiting it.

The moment, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into atoms. Light could then travel freely for the first time; that light is the cosmic microwave background.

The stretching of light to longer wavelengths. For distant galaxies it measures how much the universe has expanded since the light left: at redshift 1 everything was half as far apart as now. Higher redshift means farther away and longer ago.

The period, a few hundred million to a billion years after the Big Bang, when light from the first stars and galaxies stripped the electrons back off the hydrogen that filled space, ending the cosmic dark ages.

A narrow beam of matter shot out along the spin axis of a feeding black hole at nearly the speed of light. Jets can reach millions of light-years, far beyond the host galaxy. A blazar is one pointed at us.

Two orbiting bodies whose periods form a simple ratio, so that they keep meeting at the same places and their tugs add up. Io, Europa and Ganymede are locked 4:2:1. Pluto circles the Sun twice for every three orbits of Neptune.
The distance inside which a planet's tides pull harder on a moon than the moon's own gravity holds it together. A loosely bound moon that strays inside is pulled apart, which is one way rings form.

The size of the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole: about 3 km for each solar mass. For the Sun it would be 3 km, for the Earth 9 mm, for the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way 12.7 million km.
A measure of how unlikely a result is to be a fluke. Three sigma is about a 1-in-740 chance and is called evidence. Five sigma is about 1 in 3.5 million and is the usual bar for a discovery.
A stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun in all directions at 300 to 800 km/s. It causes auroras, shapes comet tails and fills a bubble that extends well beyond Pluto.
Light spread out by wavelength. Each element absorbs and emits at its own wavelengths, so a spectrum shows what something is made of, how hot it is and how fast it is moving.
Any object whose true brightness is known, so that how faint it looks gives its distance. Cepheid variables and one kind of supernova are the most important.
The explosion of a star. Massive stars explode when their cores collapse; white dwarfs explode when they gain too much mass from a companion. For a few weeks one can outshine its galaxy.
The expanding shell of gas left by a supernova, glowing where it ploughs into its surroundings. Remnants stay visible for tens of thousands of years and spread newly made elements through the galaxy.
Warming of a moon's interior as its planet's gravity repeatedly squeezes and stretches it. It powers Io's volcanoes and keeps the oceans of Europa and Enceladus liquid.
When a body rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same face always points at its partner. The Moon is locked to Earth, and most large moons are locked to their planets.

A planet crossing in front of its star as seen from Earth, dimming it slightly. The size of the dip gives the planet's size, and starlight filtered through its atmosphere can show what the air is made of.

For a group of objects held together by gravity and neither collapsing nor flying apart, the energy of their motion is tied to the strength of their mutual gravity. Measure how fast the members move and you can work out the total mass.
The hot, dense core left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel: about the Sun's mass in a ball the size of the Earth. It no longer fuses anything and slowly cools for billions of years.
Weakly interacting massive particle: a long-favoured candidate for dark matter, heavier than a proton and feeling only gravity and the weak nuclear force. Decades of searches have not found one.

The strip of sky hidden behind the dust and stars of the Milky Way's own disc, where galaxies beyond are hard to see in visible light. About a fifth of the extragalactic sky was unmapped until infrared and radio surveys looked through it.
